last_transition_reason: The proof establishes both directions of the claimed equivalence. It correctly rewrites the product as N(q)/D(q), counts multiplicities of primitive d-th roots of unity in N and D via the floor expressions, derives the inequality from polynomiality in the forward direction, and in the converse shows that all roots of D occur in N with at least the same multiplicity, hence D divides N over C[q]. The final step from divisibility over C[q] to a quotient in Z[q] is justified by monic long division in Z[q]. The argument matches the lemma's semantic role exactly and appears self-contained.
latest_nl_proof:
If a = b, then the product is empty, so P_{a,b,r}(q) = 1, and for every positive integer d both floor differences are 0. Thus the claim is trivial in this case.

Assume now that a < b. Since (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (q^(r+i) - 1) / (q^i - 1) for each i, write
N(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^(r+i) - 1),
D(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^i - 1).
Then P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q). Also D(q) is monic and nonconstant, because each factor q^i - 1 is monic and there is at least one factor.

For a complex number zeta and a polynomial F, let mult_zeta(F) denote the multiplicity of zeta as a root of F.

Fix a positive integer d and let zeta be a primitive d-th root of unity. For any integer m >= 1, zeta is a root of q^m - 1 exactly when d divides m. Moreover that root is simple, because (q^m - 1)' = m q^(m-1), and at zeta this derivative is m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Hence
mult_zeta(q^m - 1) = 1 if d divides m, and 0 otherwise.

Therefore
mult_zeta(D) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides i }
              = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d),
because floor(v/d) - floor(u/d) counts the multiples of d in {u+1,...,v}. Likewise,
mult_zeta(N) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides (r+i) }
              = #{ m in {r+a+1,...,r+b} : d divides m }
              = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).

Now suppose first that P_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Then N = D P_{a,b,r} in C[q]. So for every complex number zeta,
mult_zeta(N) = mult_zeta(D) + mult_zeta(P_{a,b,r}) >= mult_zeta(D).
Applying this to a primitive d-th root of unity gives
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)
for every positive integer d.

Conversely, assume that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Let zeta be any complex root of D, and let d be the order of zeta. Then zeta is a primitive d-th root of unity, so the formulas above show that mult_zeta(N) >= mult_zeta(D). Thus every root of D occurs in N with at least the same multiplicity as in D. Since over C polynomials factor into linear factors, this implies that D divides N in C[q].

Because D is monic and N,D are in Z[q], ordinary long division of N by D gives polynomials Q,R in Z[q] with
N = DQ + R,   deg R < deg D.
But D divides N in C[q], and clearly D divides DQ in C[q], so D divides R = N - DQ in C[q]. If R were nonzero, then any polynomial divisible by the nonconstant polynomial D would have degree at least deg D, contradicting deg R < deg D. Hence R = 0. So N = DQ with Q in Z[q]. Therefore
P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q) = Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

This proves the equivalence.
role_in_parent: Converts polynomiality of the shifted interval product into explicit floor inequalities counting multiples in the shifted and unshifted intervals.
statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. Then P_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q] if and only if for every positive integer d one has floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).

domain_restrictions: d ranges over positive integers only
The product index i ranges over integers between a + 1 and b inclusive
If a equals b, the product is empty and equals 1
P_{a,b,r}(q) is interpreted as an element of the polynomial ring in q with integer coefficients when the claim says it belongs to Z[q]
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For each fixed choice of integers a, b, r satisfying 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, the finite product P_{a,b,r}(q), defined as the product over i from a + 1 to b of (1 minus q to the power r plus i) divided by (1 minus q to the power i), with empty product equal to 1, is a polynomial with integer coefficients in q if and only if for every positive integer d, floor((r + b) divided by d) minus floor((r + a) divided by d) is at least floor(b divided by d) minus floor(a divided by d).
quantifier_order: Fix integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0
Define P_{a,b,r}(q) by the finite product over integers i from a + 1 to b, with empty product equal to 1
For every positive integer d, the stated floor-function inequality must hold
The claim is that the polynomial membership of P_{a,b,r}(q) is equivalent to that universal condition on d

variables.name: q
variables.role: indeterminate used to define the product

witness_dependencies: There is no existential witness in the statement; the condition is purely universal in d
The truth of the polynomial membership claim depends on checking the inequality for every positive integer d
